group.passage: In 2008 and 2009, a new kind of racing swimsuit shook the sport of swimming. Below, a swim coach and a sports scientist look back on the “super suits.”

passage_parts.label: A
passage_parts.title: A Coach’s View
passage_parts.text: During the 2009 world championships in Rome, 43 world records fell in a single week. I remember the cheering, but I also remember feeling uneasy. The newest suits were made entirely of polyurethane, a rubber-like material that kept water out and trapped air against the body, so swimmers floated higher and slipped through the water more easily. Results began to depend on what a swimmer was wearing. The clearest sign came when Michael Phelps, still in the previous year’s model, lost his first major individual race in four years to a rival in a newer, all-polyurethane suit. Many athletes were tied to sponsors, so they could not simply switch to the fastest suit on the market. Swimming’s governing body was right to ban such suits from 2010 and to limit how much of the body a suit may cover. My only complaint is that it acted so late. It had approved these suits in the first place, and the records set in them may now stand for generations, leaving young swimmers to chase marks they cannot reach.

passage_parts.label: B
passage_parts.title: A Sports Scientist Responds
passage_parts.text: I understand why so many coaches felt cheated, and the suits certainly worked. Because the power needed to push through water rises with the cube of speed, a swimmer must spend about 33 percent more energy to go just 10 percent faster, so even a small cut in drag is a real gift. Yet technology has always shaped this sport. When suits made of Lycra replaced nylon in the early 1970s, the change was almost as dramatic, yet few people today would say that records swum in Lycra do not count. Top athletes are never purely natural; their results combine talent with coaching, science, and equipment. The real problem in 2009 was not technology itself but the fact that some swimmers could not get the best of it. As for the fear that the suit-era marks would last forever, it has proved mistaken: within a short time, swimmers in legal suits began breaking those records again. Rules about equipment will always draw somewhat arbitrary lines. What matters is that every swimmer competes under the same ones.

questions.stem: On which of the following points do the two writers agree?

options.A: The suits gave the swimmers who wore them a real advantage.
options.B: The records set in the suits should be erased from the books.
options.C: Swimming’s governing body waited too long before acting.
options.D: Technology has no proper place in the sport of swimming.

questions.stem: In Text A, how does the writer present Phelps’s defeat in Rome?

options.A: As proof that a champion had stopped training seriously.
options.B: As a case of a winner breaking the rules with a banned suit.
options.C: As an example of a race whose result seemed to depend on the suits.
options.D: As an example of a sponsor forcing a swimmer into a newer suit.

questions.stem: Why does the writer of Text B mention the change from nylon to Lycra?

options.A: To show that newer materials always make swimmers faster.
options.B: To point out that records set after an earlier leap in suit design are now widely accepted.
options.C: To explain why polyurethane was banned while Lycra was allowed.
options.D: To suggest that swimmers in the 1970s were faster than most people think.

questions.stem: How would the writer of Text B most likely respond to the worry expressed at the end of Text A?

options.A: By agreeing that young swimmers may lose interest in the sport.
options.B: By arguing that the suits should never have been banned at all.
options.C: By saying that the ban came at exactly the right moment.
options.D: By noting that those records soon started to fall to swimmers in approved suits.

1.explanation_zh: Text A 說新泳衣讓選手浮得更高、在水中更順，成績開始取決於穿什麼；Text B 一開頭就承認泳衣「確實有效」，還用阻力與速度的關係說明小小的減阻就是很大的好處。兩人都認為泳衣帶來真正的優勢。其他選項都只有一方主張，或兩方都沒有主張。

translation_zh.text:
2008 和 2009 年，一種新型的競賽泳衣震撼了游泳界。以下是一位游泳教練和一位運動科學家回顧這些「超級泳衣」。
【A　教練的看法】2009 年在羅馬舉行的世界錦標賽上，短短一週就有 43 項世界紀錄被打破。我記得當時的歡呼聲，但也記得自己感到不安。最新的泳衣完全用聚氨酯製成，這種類似橡膠的材料能隔絕水，並把空氣留在身體周圍，讓選手浮得更高、在水中滑行得更輕鬆。比賽結果開始取決於選手穿什麼。最明顯的跡象是：菲爾普斯仍穿著前一年的款式，輸給了一位穿著較新、全聚氨酯泳衣的對手——這是他四年來第一次在重大個人項目中落敗。許多運動員和贊助商綁約，無法說換就換成市面上最快的泳衣。游泳的主管機關從 2010 年起禁用這類泳衣，並限制泳衣可以覆蓋身體的範圍，這是正確的。我唯一的不滿是它行動得太晚。當初正是它核准了這些泳衣，而穿著它們創下的紀錄，如今可能維持好幾代，讓年輕選手追逐永遠達不到的成績。
【B　運動科學家的回應】我明白為什麼這麼多教練覺得被欺騙了，而這些泳衣也的確有效。因為在水中前進所需的功率會隨速度的三次方增加，選手只要快 10%，就得多花大約 33% 的能量，所以即使只減少一點阻力，都是很大的好處。然而，科技一直在塑造這項運動。1970 年代初，萊卡泳衣取代尼龍泳衣，那次的改變幾乎一樣劇烈，但今天很少有人會說穿萊卡泳衣游出的紀錄不算數。頂尖運動員從來就不是純天然的；他們的成績結合了天分、訓練、科學和裝備。2009 年真正的問題不在於科技本身，而在於有些選手拿不到最好的科技。至於擔心超級泳衣時代的紀錄會永遠留著，事實證明是錯的：不久之後，穿著合規泳衣的選手就又開始打破那些紀錄。關於裝備的規定，總會劃下多少有些武斷的界線。重要的是每位選手都在同一套規則下比賽。

options: 任意的、沒有一定標準的
